source_text: (At enim in tanta, inquam, strage cadauerum nec sepeliri potuerunt. neque istud pia fides nimium reformidat, tenens praedictum nec absumentes bestias resurrecturis corporibus obfuturas, quorum capillus capitis non peribit. nullo modo diceret ueritas: nolite timere eos, qui corpus occidunt, animam autem non possunt occidere, si quidquam obesset futurae uitae quidquid inimici de corporibus occisorum facere uoluissent. nisi forte quispiam sic absurdus est, ut contendat eos, qui corpus occidunt, non debere timeri ante mortem, ne corpus occidant, et timeri debere post mortem, ne corpus occisum sepeliri non sinant. falsum est ergo quod ait: qui corpus occidunt et postea non habent quid faciant, si habent tanta, quae de cadaueribus faciant? absit, ut falsum sit quod ueritas dixit. dictum est enim aliquid eos facere, cum occidunt, quia in corpore sensus est occidendo, postea uero nihil habere quod faciant, quia nullus sensus est in corpore occiso. multa itaque corpora Christianorum terra non texit, sed nullum eorum quisquam a caelo et terra separauit, quam totam inplet praesentia sui, qui nouit unde resuscitet quod creauit. dicitur quidem in psalmo: posuerunt mortalia seruorum tuorum escam uolatilibus caeli, carnes sanctorum tuorum bestiis terrae; effuderunt sanguinem eorum tamquam aquam in circuitu Hierusalem, et non erat qui sepeliret, sed magis ad exaggerandam crudelitatem eorum, qui ista fecerunt, non ad eorum infelicitatem, qui ista perpessi sunt. quamuis enim haec in conspectu hominum dura et dira uideantur, sed pretiosa in conspectu domini mors sanctorum eius. proinde ista omnia, id est curatio funeris, conditio sepulturae, pompa exequiarum, magis sunt uiuorum solacia quam subsidia mortuorum. si aliquid prodest inpio sepultura pretiosa, oberit pio uilis aut nulla. praeclaras exequias in conspectu hominum purpurato illi diuiti turba exhibuit famulorum, sed multo clariores in conspectu domini ulceroso illi pauperi ministerium praebuit angelorum, qui eum non extulerunt in marmoreum tumulum, sed in Abrahae gremium sustulerunt. rident haec illi, contra quos defendendam suscepimus ciuitatem dei. uerum tamen sepulturae curam etiam eorum philosophi contempserunt. et saepe uniuersi exercitus, dum pro terrena patria morerentur, ubi postea iacerent uel quibus bestiis esca fierent, non curarunt, licuitque de hac re poetis plausibiliter dicere: caelo tegitur, qui non habet urnam. quanto minus debent de corporibus insepultis insultare Christianis, quibus et ipsius carnis membrorumque omnium reformatio non solum ex terra, uerum etiam ex aliorum elementorum secretissimo sinu, quo dilapsa cadauera recesserunt, in temporis puncto reddenda et redintegranda promittitur!
thought_title: Burial cannot harm the dead, and costly rites help only the living
orientation: Augustine is answering the objection that Christians killed in the sack of Rome could not be buried, continuing his argument that burial does not affect the dead.
pass_a_gloss: But in so great a slaughter of corpses, I say, they could not even be buried. And pious faith does not fear this too much, holding that it was foretold that not even the beasts that consume them will harm the bodies that are to rise, of which not a hair of the head will perish. In no way would the Truth have said: do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul, if anything that enemies might have wished to do with the bodies of the slain could harm the future life. Unless perhaps someone is so absurd that he contends that those who kill the body should not be feared before death, lest they kill the body, and should be feared after death, lest they not allow the killed body to be buried. Therefore what he said is false: those who kill the body and afterwards have nothing they can do, if they have so many things which they can do with the corpses? Far be it that what the Truth said should be false. For it was said that they do something when they kill, because there is sensation in the body while it is being killed, but afterwards they have nothing that they can do, because there is no sensation in a killed body. And so the earth did not cover many bodies of Christians, but no one separated any of them from heaven and earth, which he fills entirely with the presence of him who knows whence he may raise up what he created. It is said indeed in the psalm: they placed the mortal bodies of your servants as food for the birds of heaven, the flesh of your holy ones for the beasts of the earth; they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them, but this was said rather to exaggerate the cruelty of those who did these things, not the misery of those who suffered these things. For although these things seem hard and dreadful in the sight of men, yet precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones. Therefore all these things, that is the care of the funeral, the preparation of burial, the pomp of funeral rites, are more consolations of the living than helps of the dead. If a costly burial profits an impious man, a cheap or no burial will harm a pious man. Splendid funeral rites in the sight of men the crowd of servants displayed for that rich man clothed in purple, but far more splendid ones in the sight of the Lord the ministry of angels provided for that poor man covered with sores, who did not carry him out into a marble tomb, but lifted him into the bosom of Abraham. Those men laugh at these things, against whom we have undertaken to defend the city of God. But nevertheless even their philosophers despised the care of burial. And often whole armies, while they died for their earthly fatherland, did not care where they would afterwards lie or for which beasts they would become food, and it was permitted for poets to say plausibly about this matter: he is covered by heaven, who has no urn. How much less ought they to insult Christians about unburied bodies, to whom the restoration of the flesh itself and of all the members is promised to be returned and restored in a point of time not only from the earth, but also from the most secret bosom of the other elements, into which the fallen corpses have slipped away!

choices.why: Keeps the adjective-noun force of the Latin; 'pious' preserves the sense of dutiful reverence toward God.
Renders the present participle literally as a relative clause, preserving the active consuming force.
Conditio here means the arranging or laying out of burial; 'preparation' captures the act rather than a mere condition.
Pompa carries the sense of public display and procession; 'pomp' preserves the critical tone.
Subsidia means aids or supports; 'helps' is plain and keeps the contrast with consolations.
Sinus means a hollow or fold; 'bosom' preserves the image of a hidden containing place.

pass_b_english: "But in such a slaughter of corpses," I said, "they could not even be buried." Pious faith does not fear this too much, holding to what was foretold: that the beasts that consume them will not harm the bodies that are about to rise, whose hair of the head will not perish. The Truth would never have said, "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28), if anything that enemies might choose to do with the bodies of the slain could harm the life to come. Unless someone is so absurd as to argue that those who kill the body should not be feared before death, lest they kill the body, but should be feared after death, lest they not allow the slain body to be buried. Is it false, then, what the Truth says: "those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do" (Luke 12:4), if they have so much they can do with the corpses? Far be it that what the Truth said should be false. For it says they do something when they kill, because there is sensation in the body while it is being killed; but after that they have nothing they can do, because there is no sensation in a slain body. So the earth did not cover many bodies of Christians, but no one separated any of them from heaven and earth, which he fills entirely with his presence—he who knows from where he will raise up what he created. It is said in the psalm: "They gave the bodies of your servants as food to the birds of the air, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth; they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them" (Psalm 79:2-3). But this was said to exaggerate the cruelty of those who did these things, not the misery of those who suffered them. For though these things seem hard and dreadful in human sight, yet "precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones" (Psalm 116:15). Therefore all these things—the care of the funeral, the preparation of burial, the pomp of funeral rites—are more consolations for the living than helps for the dead. If a costly burial benefits an impious man, a cheap one or none at all would harm a pious man. A crowd of servants gave that rich man in purple a splendid funeral in human sight, but far more splendid in the sight of the Lord was the ministry the angels gave to that poor man covered with sores—they did not carry him out to a marble tomb, but lifted him up into Abraham's bosom (Luke 16:19-22). Those against whom we have undertaken to defend the city of God laugh at these things. Yet even their philosophers despised the care of burial. And often whole armies, while dying for their earthly country, did not care where they would lie afterwards or what beasts they would become food for. And the poets were allowed to say to applause on this matter: "He who has no urn is covered by the sky." How much less should they mock Christians about unburied bodies, when to Christians is promised the restoration and renewal not only of the flesh itself and all its members from the earth, but also from the most secret bosom of the other elements into which the scattered corpses have slipped away—to be given back in a moment of time!

problems.quote: Is it false, then, what he says
problems.why: Source states 'therefore it is false what he says' as an opponent's claim Augustine refutes; English frames it as a question, changing the rhetorical structure.
problems.fix: Therefore it is false what he says
problems.ruling: Source 'falsum est ergo' is declarative, not interrogative. English question changes Augustine's rhetorical force.

problems.quote: For though these things seem hard and dreadful in human sight
problems.source_quote: quamuis enim haec in conspectu hominum dura et dira uideantur, sed
problems.why: Source has 'sed' after 'uideantur' connecting to next clause; English renders as 'For though...but' splitting the construction incorrectly.
problems.fix: For though these things seem hard and dreadful in human sight, yet
problems.ruling: Source 'quamuis...sed' is concessive clause + main clause; English 'For though...but' creates grammatical error.

problems.quote: If a costly burial benefits an impious man, then a cheap one or none at all will harm a pious man.
problems.source_quote: si aliquid prodest inpio sepultura pretiosa, oberit pio uilis aut nulla.
problems.why: Source is a rhetorical question expecting 'no'; English states it as fact, reversing Augustine's argument that burial doesn't harm the pious.
problems.fix: If a costly burial benefits an impious man, would a cheap one or none at all harm a pious man?
problems.ruling: Source is rhetorical question; English declarative reverses Augustine's argument that burial status is irrelevant.

problems.quote: And the poets were allowed to say plausibly on this matter
problems.source_quote: licuitque de hac re poetis plausibiliter dicere
problems.why: 'plausibiliter' means 'to applause' or 'applaudably'; 'plausibly' is a false friend, suggesting logical probability rather than popular approval.
problems.fix: And the poets were allowed to say to applause on this matter
problems.ruling: 'plausibiliter' = 'to applause/applaudably' in classical Latin; 'plausibly' as 'logically probable' misleads readers.

problems.source_quote: posuerunt mortalia seruorum tuorum escam uolatilibus caeli, carnes sanctorum tuorum bestiis terrae; effuderunt sanguinem eorum tamquam aquam in circuitu Hierusalem, et non erat qui sepeliret
problems.why: Augustine uses Septuagint numbering; this is Psalm 78:2-3 in Hebrew numbering, not 79.
problems.ruling: Augustine cites Psalm 78 (Hebrew) not 79; wrong scripture reference misleads the reader.

problems.source_quote: pretiosa in conspectu domini mors sanctorum eius
problems.why: Augustine uses Septuagint numbering; this is Psalm 115:15 in Hebrew numbering, not 116.
problems.ruling: Augustine cites Psalm 115 (Hebrew) not 116; wrong scripture reference misleads the reader.

problems.quote: would a cheap one or none at all harm a pious man?
problems.why: English adds question mark, turning statement into rhetorical question; Latin is declarative: 'a cheap or no burial will harm a pious man.'
problems.fix: a cheap one or none at all will harm a pious man.
problems.ruling: Latin 'oberit pio uilis aut nulla' is declarative: a cheap or no burial WILL harm a pious man. English question mark inverts the meaning.

would a cheap one or none at all harm a pious man?: Latin 'oberit pio uilis aut nulla' is declarative, not a rhetorical question, so changed to 'a cheap one or none at all will harm a pious man.'

problems.quote: a cheap one or none at all will harm a pious man
problems.why: The English 'will harm' is wrong. 'Oberit' = 'will harm/burden', but the logic is conditional: 'If costly burial benefits the impious, then cheap/none will harm the pious' — this is a reductio ad absurdum. The English loses the conditional force and presents it as Augustine's actual claim, when it's part of a rhetorical argument he rejects.
problems.fix: a cheap one or none at all would harm a pious man

fixed: Changed 'will harm' to 'would harm' to restore the conditional force of the reductio ad absurdum: 'oberit pio uilis aut nulla' follows from the hypothetical 'si aliquid prodest inpio sepultura pretiosa'.
